title: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
gist: Polestar and the University of Oxford ran a 12-driver pilot study that instrumented drivers (heart rate, EEG skullcaps, gaze tracking) on the Gotland Ring to quantify how performance feels: the 536 hp dual-motor Polestar 4 delivered 32% higher peak acceleration and 15% less steering effort than the single-motor car and scored 93 vs 77.9 for overall experience. Gitlin uses it, plus quotes from ex-Ford CTO Richard Parry-Jones and GM's Ken Morris, to argue that customers who never ask about handling still reward it.

themes.theme: Polestar-Oxford pilot study: measuring how performance feels

insights.claim: Polestar and University of Oxford researchers ran a pilot study in which 12 drivers track-tested rear-drive and all-wheel-drive Polestar 4s on Sweden's Gotland Ring while wearing heart rate monitors and electrode skullcaps, with the cars' gaze-tracking driver monitoring, telemetry, and post-drive interviews also recorded.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: OEMs are starting to treat driver physiology as a measurable product attribute, which could become a new marketing and differentiation lever for EVs whose spec-sheet numbers are converging.

insights.claim: The dual-motor Polestar 4, with 536 hp (400 kW) or double the single-motor version's power, produced 32 percent higher peak acceleration and needed 15 percent less steering effort than the single-motor car on a matched fast lap.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Doubling motor count buys measurable gains in both acceleration and driver workload, which supports pricing premiums on dual-motor trims.
insights.locator: You won’t be surprised to learn

insights.claim: On a 0-100 scale, drivers rated the AWD Polestar 4 89.2 for performance and 93 for overall experience, versus 67.7 and 77.9 for the rear-drive version, and described the faster car as building trust, control, and deep engagement, likened to a controlled roller coaster.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The subjective gap (about 15 points overall) is the kind of number that could justify upsell to performance trims.

insights.claim: Oxford researcher Max Klapow frames performance as giving the driver confidence and control through predictable vehicle responses rather than simply going faster.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Shifts the EV performance contest away from the 0-60 arms race toward controllability, which is harder to commoditize.
insights.quote: “Performance is not simply about going faster. It is about giving the driver a sense of confidence and control through predictable vehicle responses,”

insights.claim: The Polestar study has only 12 participants and is explicitly a pilot, so its findings are suggestive rather than conclusive.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Treat it as marketing-adjacent research, not robust evidence.

themes.theme: EV performance arms race and spec-sheet limits

insights.claim: Gitlin argues performance EVs are in an arms race to minimize 0-60 mph times, while acceleration, top speed, and lap times are easy to measure but miss the effect of performance on the driver.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: When every EV is quick, straight-line acceleration stops differentiating and brands need other attributes to compete on.
insights.locator: Acceleration, top speed, and lap times

insights.claim: The Polestar 4, which Gitlin calls a compelling Porsche Macan alternative, can no longer be bought in the US.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Polestar's US product line has shrunk, limiting its exposure to the US EV market.

themes.theme: Handling as a hidden driver of customer satisfaction

insights.claim: Former Ford CTO Richard Parry-Jones said that by tracking customer satisfaction against attributes like steering, brakes, and spaciousness, he proved steering was the most strongly correlated attribute because bad steering is tiring, even though customers never asked about it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Spending on chassis and steering tuning can pay off in satisfaction and loyalty even when buyers can't put it into words, so it is a moat that is easy to underrate.
insights.quote: I was able to prove that steering was the most strongly correlated, because bad steering is tiring.

insights.claim: Gitlin's contrarian takeaway is that even people who say handling doesn't matter still prefer a car that handles well, which supports automakers spending on vehicle dynamics that customers never ask for.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Cost-cutting on chassis tuning may hurt brand preference in ways that surveys asking customers what they want will not catch.

insights.claim: GM's Ken Morris says customers can absolutely feel handling differences even if they can't name them, describing a car as feeling 'like a vault', and that engineers deliberately tune parts toward that outcome.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Incumbents treat structural feel as a deliberate engineering edge, which could set them apart from cost-focused EV newcomers.
